t: she designated her vow and said to the priest, "These are for my vow and these are for my obligation". She brought the priest four birds and said which of them are for her vow and which for her obligation.

and he does not know which of them he offered above etc.. There is concern that the two voluntary burnt-offerings were offered below (and she has not fulfilled the obligation of offering them), and the two obligatory birds were offered above (and she has not fulfilled the obligation of the sin-offering). She must therefore bring two more birds for a burnt-offering and one for a sin-offering (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kinnim 3:5).

and all three are offered above. So it reads in the manuscripts, but it seems to be a scribal error and should read "and the two are offered above", while the third, which comes for her sin-offering, is offered below (Kiryat Sefer, Radbaz, Kesef Mishneh).

but if they were of two kinds. She brought two turtledoves and two young pigeons and said that one pair is for her vow, for example she said the two turtledoves are for her vow. The priest offered one kind above and the other kind below.

she brings four others, two of the kind in which she designated her vow, which are offered for her vow. Two turtledoves are offered above as a burnt-offering for her vow, in case the first turtledoves were offered below.

and two of whichever kind she wishes shall be for her obligation, one offered above and one below. If at first her two young pigeons of obligation were offered above, she has not fulfilled the obligation of the sin-offering; and if they were offered below, she has not fulfilled the obligation of the burnt-offering (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).
she fixed her vow. She fixed, at the time of the vow, which kind she would bring for the bird burnt-offerings of her vow.
and she brought four birds etc.. Of the same kind.

and he does not know which was offered above and which was offered below. This speaks of a case where, at the time of bringing, she specified which pair is for her obligation and which for her vow (Radbaz, Merkevet HaMishneh).

she must bring two turtledoves and two young pigeons for her vow. For even if the kind she brought is the kind she fixed for her vow, there is still concern that the pair she designated as a burnt-offering was offered below and disqualified. She must therefore bring a pair of each kind and offer them above as a burnt-offering.

and she brings one young bird to complete her obligation. Perhaps the two that she offered below were the birds she designated for her vow, and she has not fulfilled the sin-offering. But she does not need an additional bird to fulfill the obligatory burnt-offering, for if the birds first offered above were the voluntary birds (and of the voluntary kind), she fulfills the obligatory burnt-offering with one of the four burnt-offerings she now brings; and if the birds offered above were not her voluntary birds, she already fulfilled the burnt-offering by offering them (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).

and it is offered above, for he already offered two below, which are the sin-offering. The commentators found these words of the Rambam difficult. Some emended them in accordance with the Commentary on the Mishnah to "and it is offered below" and deleted the end of the halakhah (Kiryat Sefer, Radbaz; and see Merkevet HaMishneh and Har HaMoriah, who strained to explain the reading before us).
but if they were of two kinds. The priest offered one kind above and the other kind below, and he does not remember what he offered above and what he offered below.
two turtledoves and two young pigeons for her vow. For she fixed her vow and does not remember which kind she fixed, so she must bring both kinds for her vow.

and she brings for her obligation two turtledoves or two young pigeons, to be offered one above and one below. Since she does not know what was offered above and what below, she cannot fulfill her obligation with the birds first offered, and must bring a complete nest for her obligation.
and likewise if she gave them to the priest and forgot what she gave him. She fixed her vow and forgot which kind she fixed, and she gave the priest four birds and forgot which kind she gave him.

she brings two turtledoves etc.. It is not known where what she brought was offered, so she did not fulfill her obligation at all by the first offering, and she must bring a nest for the obligation and both kinds for her vow.

she fixed her obligation. She fixed whether she would bring a nest for her obligation, as in the offering of a poor woman after childbirth, or a lamb for a burnt-offering and a bird for a sin-offering, as in the offering of a wealthy woman after childbirth (for a poor woman who brought the offering of a wealthy woman has fulfilled her obligation, Hilchot Shegagot 10:13).
and she fixed her vow. Two turtledoves or two young pigeons.
four for her vow. Two turtledoves and two young pigeons, and they are offered above as a burnt-offering.

and two for her obligation. Turtledoves or young pigeons, and they are offered one as a sin-offering and one as a burnt-offering, and she fulfills her obligation with them if she fixed a nest for her obligation.
and she also brings one sin-offering, a young pigeon or a turtledove, with the lamb. And she fulfills her obligation with them if she fixed a lamb and a bird for her obligation.
and none of these sin-offerings is eaten, because they are of doubtful status. A bird sin-offering brought for a doubt is not eaten (above 7:10).
even though he did not take the handful. The disqualified one, but rather the qualified one.

and likewise if he gathered the frankincense. After taking the handful, one gathers from the meal-offering all the frankincense that was placed on it, and offers it up together with the handful on the altar (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 13:12).

if a fit person took the handful and gave it to an unfit one etc.. After taking the handful, the handful is transferred from one service vessel to another service vessel in order to sanctify it for burning on the altar. This act must be done by a fit priest and with the right hand.
a pebble. A small stone. In all the cases here the handful has become deficient and is disqualified.

he must again take the handful inside. He returns the handful he took to the meal-offering and takes the handful again in the Temple court (Hazon Yechezkel, Menachot 5:7). Some say that the handful he took is disqualified and is not returned to the meal-offering; rather he takes a handful from the remainder of the meal-offering after completing its measure, as below in halakhah 15 (Arukh HaShulchan 141:12; and see Radbaz, who discusses both possibilities).
the handful was scattered on the floor. After it was sanctified in a service vessel (Kesef Mishneh; compare above 1:25).
the meal-offering was not in a service vessel. At the time the handful was taken from it.
that its handful was not in a service vessel. He did not place the handful in a service vessel.

that he brought it up to the altar not in a service vessel. He brought the handful of the meal-offering up by hand or in a non-sacred vessel (and if he brought the handful up in a service vessel and threw it onto the altar fire by hand while fit, Radbaz as above 2:24).

that he mixed it with its oil outside the Temple court. After the fine flour of the meal-offerings is placed in a vessel, it is mixed with oil (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 13:5). Although if he did not mix at all the meal-offering is valid (ibid. halakhah 11), if he mixed outside it is disqualified.
all the meal-offerings on which oil was poured. For some meal-offerings, additional oil is poured on the meal-offering after the mixing (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 13:5-7).
he broke them into pieces. All the baked meal-offerings are broken into pieces after baking (ibid. halakhah 10).

he salted them. He salted the meal-offering itself (for example in a priest's meal-offering, which is burned entirely and salted entirely; but this does not speak of salting the handful, which is disqualified if done by a non-priest, Radbaz).
he presented them. All meal-offerings must be presented at the southwest corner of the altar before they are offered (ibid. 12:6).
he waved them. The meal-offering of the suspected adulteress and the omer meal-offering are waved (ibid.).

and if the priest did not present or wave them, they are valid. Presenting and waving do not invalidate; they are a commandment to be done ab initio (and so too the mixing and breaking into pieces, ibid. 13:11).
he left out its oil. For every meal-offering one log of oil is to be put for each issaron (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 12:7).
he left out its frankincense. For every meal-offering one handful of frankincense is to be put (ibid.).
two kortei of frankincense. Two small pieces.
a sinner's meal-offering. It is forbidden to put oil and frankincense on it (ibid.).
if he put oil on it... it is disqualified. Because the oil is absorbed in it and it is impossible to remove all of it.
it was finely ground. Ground fine.

it is disqualified out of doubt, since it is impossible to gather it out. The doubt is whether only a mixture that is absorbed into the meal-offering, like oil, disqualifies, or whether a mixture that cannot be removed from the meal-offering also disqualifies.

"dry" is said only in contrast to oil. In the verse "every meal-offering mixed with oil or dry...", the sinner's meal-offering is called "dry" relative to other meal-offerings that are mixed with oil, and not relative to being dry of water.
a meal-offering from which the handful was taken twice is valid. He burned the handful in two stages (see Kesef Mishneh and Mishneh LaMelekh).
for salt is indispensable for a meal-offering, as we have explained. Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:12.
a meal-offering that became deficient before the taking of the handful. It became deficient from the measure in which the meal-offering must be offered.
he brings from his own house and fills it up. He adds non-sacred fine flour and joins it to the meal-offering.

for the taking of the handful is what fixes it. And if it was deficient from the measure of the meal-offering at the time of taking the handful, the meal-offering is disqualified (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 12:5).
he volunteered a handful of frankincense on its own. That it be burned on the altar (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 14:1), and its measure is at least a handful (ibid. 16:13).

and likewise the two bowls of frankincense that go with the bread. On the table, next to the rows of the showbread, two vessels were placed, each containing a handful of frankincense (Hilchot Temidin U'Musafin 5:2). The frankincense was burned on the altar every Shabbat (ibid. halakhah 5).
until there are two handfuls from beginning to end. For the bowls must be placed with the bread on the table from the previous Shabbat (see there halakhot 12-13).
he set aside two handfuls for one meal-offering. He set aside a double amount of frankincense for the meal-offering.
and one of them was lost. And now there is less than two handfuls.

before the taking of the handful it was not fixed. Since it was lost before the handful was taken (and the same applies if it was removed, Har HaMoriah, and see Even HaAzel), its belonging to the meal-offering was not fixed, and the meal-offering is not disqualified for having too much frankincense (above halakhah 9).

before the removal of the bread they were not fixed, and they are valid etc.. Removing the bread and bowls from the table is like taking the handful from the meal-offerings: if at the time of removal the frankincense in the bowls was in excess, they are disqualified, and if it decreased earlier, they are valid.
the tzitz makes it acceptable. Through the tzitz (the High Priest's forehead plate) the offering goes up favorably and the owners fulfill their obligation with it.
the tzitz does not make it acceptable. The meal-offering is disqualified (for a similar law see above 1:34-35).

if there was a partition at the bottom of a vessel holding an issaron of meal-offering etc.. The entire meal-offering must be joined in one vessel when the handful is taken (Bavli, Menachot 24a). A vessel whose bottom part is divided in two by a partition is considered two vessels, and one may not take a handful from it even if the meal-offering in the two parts of the vessel is joined at the top.
he divided the issaron into one vessel. He separated the meal-offering in the vessel into two.
it is a doubt whether the vessel joins it for the taking of the handful. Whether the vessel considers the meal-offering in it as joined so that a handful may be taken from it.

corresponding to the height of the row of showbread. The loaves on the table were placed in two stacks (rows). The table sanctifies the handful placed on it only up to the height of the rows of bread.

the table sanctified it to be disqualified etc.. The table sanctifies the handful as if it had been placed in a service vessel (so that it is disqualified if deficient and the like), but does not make it fit for burning. It is possible that this means that the handful is disqualified by being placed on the table, and placing it afterwards in a service vessel does not help (Neum David).

he stuck the handful to the side of the vessel and took a handful. He did not take the handful from the meal-offering lying at the bottom of the vessel, but stuck it up on the side of the vessel and took the handful from there.
he turned the vessel over onto his hand and took the handful from inside it with its mouth facing down. He took a handful from a meal-offering stuck to the bottom of the vessel and lying upside down.
and he set aside another portion in its place. To complete the measure of the issaron.

and the lost one was found, and now all three are placed in one vessel and do not touch each other. The vessel joins the parts of the meal-offering that were meant to be joined together (the first and the second that was lost, the first and the third that was set aside in place of the lost one), and does not join the parts that were not meant to be joined (the second and the third). If one of the parts becomes impure, what is meant to be joined with it is also disqualified.
if the first part became impure, the lost one and the one set aside in its place are joined. And all the parts are disqualified.

and likewise with regard to taking the handful. Taking the handful from one of the parts of the meal-offering applies to that part and to the part joined with it, and permits their remainders to be eaten (see Radbaz and others, who found this difficult in light of what was said above in halakhah 23, that when a meal-offering is placed in a vessel and its parts do not touch each other, its remainders are not eaten).
and the one set aside is not eaten. For its law is like that of a meal-offering from which a handful was not taken.

if he took the handful from the first, neither of them is eaten, according to etc.. In this case both parts are joined to the part from which the handful was taken, but since the handful was taken for one issaron it permits only one issaron to be eaten, and both parts remain forbidden out of doubt, perhaps they are the part that was not permitted.
and how is this handful offered, when before him is an issaron and a half. And this meal-offering must be only one issaron.
and the parts do not touch each other. And therefore the priest can determine in his mind that he is taking the handful only for two of the three parts.
the handful got mixed with the priests' meal-offering etc.. For these meal-offerings are not subject to the taking of a handful but are burned entirely on the altar.
if he can take a handful from this one by itself and from that one by itself. If parts of each meal-offering remained that were not mixed, and he can take a handful from them.
the one from which the handful was taken counts for its owners. For in the end its handful was burned on the altar.
its handful got mixed with its remainders. The remainders of the meal-offerings are not to be burned (see above 3:16).

or its remainders got mixed with the remainders of another. Before he burned the handful. In this case the mixed remainders are considered lost (above halakhah 20), and are not to be burned ab initio (Or Sameach, Har HaMoriah; and some wrote that the text here should read "its handful got mixed with its remainders or with the remainders of another", speaking of a handful that got mixed with remainders, Likkutei Halakhot, Menachot 23b).
the two loaves. The two loaves waved on the festival of Shavuot with two lambs; the measure of each loaf is an issaron (Hilchot Temidin U'Musafin 8:3).
and the showbread. The measure of each loaf is two issarons (ibid. 5:2).
and the waved omer. A barley meal-offering brought with the omer offering on the 16th of Nisan; its measure is an issaron (ibid. 7:12).
the loaves of the thanksgiving-offering. With the thanksgiving-offering one brings forty loaves from twenty issarons of fine flour (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 9:17).
and the wafers of the nazirite. The nazirite brings with the ram of peace-offerings twenty loaves from six and two-thirds issarons (ibid. halakhah 23).

if they became deficient before the blood of the sacrifice was sprinkled, they are disqualified etc.. If they became deficient before the blood of the offering they accompany was sprinkled, they are disqualified; and if they became deficient afterwards, they are valid.
the two rows. The two stacks of the showbread.

that became deficient before the bowls were burned etc.. Along with the loaves, two bowls of frankincense were placed on the table. When the bread was removed from the table the bowls were burned on the altar and then the loaves were permitted for eating. If the loaves became deficient before the bowls were burned, the bowls are not burned for them and the loaves are disqualified.
the libations. The wine and fine flour brought with burnt-offerings and peace-offerings.

that became deficient, whether after the sacrifice was offered or before it was offered etc.. The sacrifice is not offered on specific libations, and the libations do not hold up its offering (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 2:12). Therefore even if the libations were deficient at the time of the sacrifice, the sacrifice and libations are valid, and their measure must be completed and brought.

if it was disqualified at the slaughter, the libations were not sanctified to be offered etc.. At the slaughter of the sacrifice the libations are sanctified for offering with that sacrifice. Therefore if the sacrifice was disqualified at the slaughter, the libations were not sanctified for offering with it and it is permitted to pour them with another sacrifice (Har HaMoriah).
if it was disqualified from the receiving onward. In the services after the slaughter.
slaughtered. Having been slaughtered.

they are treated as if they were disqualified by being left overnight, and they are burned. He waits until they are disqualified by being left overnight and burns them (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Zevachim 7:4; Radbaz explained that he burns them immediately).

because the court stipulates concerning them. In a communal offering the Sages intended in advance that if it turns out to be disqualified, even after the slaughter, the libations are not sanctified for offering specifically with this sacrifice, but one can still sanctify them and pour them with another slaughtered sacrifice.

and all sacrifices that were slaughtered not for their own sake etc.. All sacrifices (except the sin-offering and Passover offering) that were slaughtered in the name of another sacrifice or not for the sake of their owners are valid, but the owners have not fulfilled their obligation with them (below 15:1). Their libations must be brought with them.
the offspring of a thanksgiving-offering. The offspring of sanctified animals are offered like their mothers (Hilchot Temurah 4:1).
and its substitute. If one said of a non-sacred animal that it be the substitute for a thanksgiving-offering animal, both animals are holy with the sanctity of a thanksgiving-offering (ibid. 3:1).

if he brought them after he had atoned with the first thanksgiving-offering etc.. Since he already offered a thanksgiving-offering with bread, he does not bring bread with the second thanksgiving-offering.
and its replacement. The animal set aside in place of the lost one.

both of them require bread. Since he has not yet been atoned, both animals are fit for a thanksgiving-offering and require bread. He brings the bread with the first one he offers (Har HaMoriah, Hazon Ish).

in what case is this said? In one who vowed a thanksgiving-offering. When he said, "I take upon myself a thanksgiving-offering", he obligated himself to bring the sacrifice (and not necessarily with a particular animal). Therefore when he offers another animal instead of the thanksgiving-offering he originally sanctified, he fulfills his vow with it, and brings the thanksgiving loaves with it.

but a voluntary thanksgiving-offering etc.. When he said of an animal, "This is a thanksgiving-offering", he obligated himself to bring specifically this animal, and he does not fulfill his voluntary offering with another animal. Therefore the replacement and substitute of the thanksgiving-offering are considered a new thanksgiving-offering that he sanctified, and he must bring thanksgiving loaves for it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 7:4).

and its offspring does not require bread. For the offspring is considered a "surplus of a thanksgiving-offering", which is offered as a thanksgiving-offering and does not require thanksgiving loaves (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid., and see below halakhah 10).

and the earlier ones were found, and now all three are standing etc.. He set aside the second in place of the first, and the third in place of the second. Therefore when he offers the first as a thanksgiving-offering, he exempts the second (set aside in its place) from the bread, but does not exempt the third (which came in place of the second). Likewise when he offers the third as a thanksgiving-offering (brought in place of the second and unrelated to the first), he exempts the second but not the first. But when he offers the second as a thanksgiving-offering, he exempts both.

and with the rest he brings a thanksgiving-offering, which does not require bread. With the money that remains he buys another animal and offers it as a thanksgiving-offering, but does not bring bread with it.
but it does require libations. Like any peace-offering.
and afterwards it was found, he brings a thanksgiving-offering with the money, without bread. And the first animal he offers with bread.

this is a thanksgiving-offering. "This is" is the language of a voluntary offering, and he is not responsible for it; if the animal was lost or died he need not bring another (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 14:5).
if the bread was lost, he brings other bread. Since the thanksgiving-offering exists it must be offered, and bread must be brought with it.
if the thanksgiving-offering was lost, he does not bring another thanksgiving-offering. With the bread that was set aside.

he set aside money for his thanksgiving-offering and some remained, he brings etc.. The thanksgiving loaves are also called "thanksgiving-offering", so he may bring them from thanksgiving-offering money; but from the bread money he cannot bring the animal, since the animal is not called bread (Bavli, Menachot 80b).
this is a thanksgiving-offering. A voluntary thanksgiving-offering.

and it got mixed with its substitute etc.. From here it seems that bread is not brought with the substitute of a voluntary thanksgiving-offering. The commentators found this difficult, since above in halakhah 8 it said that the replacement and substitute of a voluntary thanksgiving-offering require bread, and some suggested deleting the word "and its substitute" there (Radbaz, and see Hazon Ish, who resolved it differently).

a thanksgiving-offering one of whose loaves was broken. With the thanksgiving-offering one brings four kinds of loaves, ten loaves of each kind. The loaves must be whole at the time of the slaughter of the thanksgiving-offering, and if one loaf was broken after the slaughter, all the loaves are disqualified.
the loaf went out. Of the Temple court.
the rest of the loaves are valid. And he eats them (and see also below 17:13).

its bread was broken or became impure or went out before the thanksgiving-offering was slaughtered, he brings other bread. Before the slaughter, even if one of the loaves was broken, the other loaves are valid, and he joins other loaves to the remaining ones.

and if after it was slaughtered it was broken or became impure or went out... all the bread is disqualified. This speaks of a case where all the loaves were disqualified, but if only some of them became impure or went out, the rest are valid, as explained at the beginning of the halakhah (Kesef Mishneh; and see Radbaz, who explained it differently).

the blood is sprinkled and the meat is eaten, and all the bread is disqualified, and he has not fulfilled his vow. Since at the time the blood was sprinkled the loaves were not fit, they are disqualified and he does not fulfill the obligation of a thanksgiving-offering with this sacrifice. The sacrifice itself, however, is valid as a peace-offering (Bavli, Menachot 46a).

the blood was sprinkled and afterwards some of the bread was broken or became impure or went out, he separates a portion etc.. After the blood of the thanksgiving-offering is sprinkled, one loaf from each kind is given as a gift to the priest, and the rest of the loaves are eaten by the owners. The loaf separated must be whole (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 9:22). When one loaf has been disqualified, one separates one of the fit loaves of the same kind.

a thanksgiving-offering slaughtered on eighty loaves, forty of the eighty were not sanctified. Each thanksgiving-offering is slaughtered on only forty loaves and one cannot sanctify more (for a similar law concerning the two loaves, see Hilchot Temidin U'Musafin 8:12).
and he raises one from each kind. He gives the priest one from each kind of those forty loaves.
and the second forty are redeemed and become non-sacred. The remaining loaves must be redeemed from their sanctity of value, and after redemption they have the status of non-sacred food.
Beit Pagi. A place in Jerusalem near the Temple Mount where the thanksgiving loaves were baked (Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 7:3).
the surface of the bread was crusted in the oven. The side stuck to the wall of the oven hardened.

and it was disqualified at its slaughter by an intention regarding time or an intention regarding place. At the time of slaughter he intended to offer or eat the sacrifice after its time or outside its proper place (below 13:1).
it was found to have a blemish or to be a treifah. Since the disqualification existed even before the slaughter, it was not sanctified by the slaughter (Bavli, Menachot 78b).

that was slaughtered not for its own sake. In this case the sacrifice is valid (see below 15:1), but since it was not slaughtered as a thanksgiving-offering, the bread is not sanctified (see Rashi, manuscript, Menachot 78b).
and the same law applies to the nazirite's ram with its bread. All the laws that apply to the thanksgiving loaves (Har HaMoriah, Arukh HaShulchan 144:19).

intentions... that disqualify sacrifices. The one offering the sacrifice must think, during the services of slaughter and offering, of the sake of the sacrifice (that he is offering this sacrifice as a sin-offering, burnt-offering and the like) and of the sake of the owners of the sacrifice, and if he offered it without specifying and did not think of the sacrifice and its owner, it is valid and the owner has fulfilled his obligation (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 4:10). But if he had an incorrect intention, sometimes his intention disqualifies the sacrifice.
or he slaughters it for the sake of a burnt-offering and for peace-offerings, or etc.. At the beginning of the slaughter he thought of one sacrifice, and afterwards of another sacrifice.
this is the intention of changing the name. The laws of this intention will be explained below in chapter 15.
in order to sprinkle its blood. This includes an intention concerning the pouring of the remainder of the blood (see below 17:6).
outside the place of its eating. The most holy offerings outside the Temple court, and the lesser sacrifices outside Jerusalem.
these are called sacrifices slaughtered outside their place. These sacrifices are disqualified and it is forbidden to eat them (below 18:3).
after the sun sets. After sunset.
that is not... and these are called piggul. And one who eats them is liable to karet (below 18:6).
from oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages in the interpretation of the verses.

it speaks only of one who intends etc.. Although the plain sense of the verse seems to speak of one who eats from the sacrifice after its time, and about this it says, "it shall not be accepted for the one who offers it... it shall be piggul", the Sages received by tradition that it speaks of a sacrifice about which, at the time of its offering, they intended to eat it on the third day, after its time.
one who intends at the time of offering to eat from it on the third day. After the end of the time for eating (peace-offerings are eaten for two days, Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 10:6).
and likewise if he intended to burn on the altar from it something fit for burning. This also includes sprinkling the blood (Commentary on the Mishnah, Zevachim 2:3).
what remains is called nothar and it is forbidden to eat it. And one is liable to karet for eating it (below 18:10).
and the sacrifice has already been accepted and atoned. Although the meat was disqualified when it became nothar, the owners have fulfilled their obligation with the offering of this sacrifice.
once the blood reached the altar properly, the owners were atoned. Even though the meat was not eaten.

only something that has permitters can become piggul. One is liable to karet for piggul only for eating something that was permitted for eating by man or for the altar by a prior act performed on another part of the sacrifice (the "permitter"). For example, the sacrificial fats, which are permitted for burning by the sprinkling of the blood, or the remainders of the meal-offering, which are permitted for eating by the burning of the handful and frankincense. But something fit for the altar without anything else permitting it (such as the blood, or the meal-offering of libations and the priest's meal-offering, which are burned entirely on the altar), one is not liable to karet for eating it as piggul, even if an intention outside its time was held concerning the sacrifice.
as will be explained. Below 18:7-8.
whether a sacrifice about which he intended etc.. The same law applies to all of them.

and a bird in two things, the pinching and the squeezing out of the blood. With a bird the pinching takes the place of the slaughter, and the squeezing out of the blood takes the place of the sprinkling, and there is no receiving of its blood (since the blood goes directly from the bird's neck) or carrying (since the bird is pinched on the altar).

and the meal-offerings from which a handful is taken. But the priests' meal-offering and the meal-offering of libations are not subject to the taking of a handful but are burned entirely, and therefore they cannot become piggul, since they have no permitters.

in the taking of the handful, the placing of the handful in a service vessel, the carrying of the handful to the altar, and its throwing onto the fire. These acts in meal-offerings correspond to the slaughter, receiving of the blood, carrying, and sprinkling done in sacrifices.
but if he had the intention during other acts. While performing other acts besides those mentioned.
flaying. The skin of the sacrifice.
cutting up. Cutting up the limbs of the burnt-offering.
mixing the meal-offering. With oil.
presenting it. Bringing the meal-offering near the southwest corner.
that intention is of no effect. The intention does not disqualify the sacrifice in any way.

to leave the blood of the sacrifice or its fats until the next day or to take them outside the Temple court. Since he did not intend to sprinkle the blood or burn the fats the next day or outside, but merely to leave them, this intention is not considered an intention outside its time or place.
to sprinkle the blood on the ramp not opposite the base etc.. And if he actually sprinkles the blood not in its proper place on the altar, the meat of the sacrifice is disqualified (see above 2:10).
to bring the blood of a sin-offering inside. Into the Sanctuary building, and such an act disqualifies the sacrifice (above 2:13).
that the impure will offer it, or others disqualified for service. Those who disqualify the sacrifice by their service (above 1:27).
to mix the blood of the sacrifice with the blood of disqualified sacrifices. To disqualify the blood (above 2:23).

to break the bones of the Passover offering and to eat from it raw. The Passover offering must be eaten roasted and it is forbidden to eat it raw (Hilchot Korban Pesach 8:4), and it is forbidden to break its bones (ibid. 10:1).

to burn a sin-offering that is burned, outside its time or outside its place. The inner sin-offerings must be burned outside Jerusalem at the place called Beit HaDeshen (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:4). If he intended to burn them after their time (the day after the slaughter) or not in their place, they are not disqualified by this intention, for their burning is not considered "eating of the altar" (above halakhah 2), for which an intention disqualifies.

in all these intentions and the like, the sacrifice is valid. Although for some of these intentions, had he actually done what he intended, the sacrifice would have been disqualified, the intention alone does not disqualify the sacrifice.
we have already explained. Above 1:23.

that carrying not on foot is not carrying etc.. Bringing the blood close to the altar by hand without walking with it does not count as carrying, and therefore a disqualifying intention at that time does not disqualify the sacrifice.
and one who walks in a place where he does not need to. Moves away from the altar with the blood.
but the intention of the owner of the sacrifice is of no effect. It does not disqualify the sacrifice in any way.
for even if we heard the owners making it piggul. That is, they stated explicitly that their intention was to offer in order to eat outside its time.

he did not disqualify it by his intention, because he is not fit for the service. The intention disqualifies the sacrifice only when there is no disqualification from some other cause (Commentary on the Mishnah, Zevachim 3:1).

and the blood that he received or the part of it that he sprinkled is poured into the channel. This blood was disqualified by the disqualified service and is poured into the drainage channel in the Temple court like all disqualified blood (see above 2:11).
the blood of life. The blood through which the life departs, which is the blood fit for the altar.
for slaughter is valid when done by the disqualified, as we have explained. Above 1:1.
there are sacrifices that are valid if done not for their own sake, as will be explained. Below 15:1.
therefore if one who is not fit for service received the blood in them. And had an intention to change the name of the sacrifice.

he disqualified the sacrifice as if he had done it for its own sake, since he is disqualified. The disqualified person who served disqualifies the sacrifice even when he served with an intention of changing the name.

and even though there is blood of life, and a fit person came back and received and sprinkled, the sacrifice was already disqualified, as we have explained. Above 1:28. This speaks here of an impure person who disqualifies the remaining blood left in the animal's neck (as explained there). But other disqualified persons do not disqualify the blood of life that remains (Keren Orah, Zevachim 26b, Har HaMoriah).
the omer meal-offering. The meal-offering of an issaron of barley flour brought with the omer offering on the 16th of Nisan.
if he took its handful not for its own sake, it is as if done for its own sake. An intention does not disqualify it.

and barley is not something fit for other sacrifices. All other meal-offerings come from wheat, and therefore barley is considered not fit for a sacrifice (and see Merkevet HaMishneh, Or Sameach and others as to why an intention is effective in the meal-offering of the suspected adulteress, which is also from barley).

one who intends during the meal-offering of jealousy with frankincense on it. For on the meal-offering of a suspected adulteress ("jealousy") it is forbidden to put frankincense (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 12:7), and therefore when frankincense is on it, it is considered unfit for service, and a disqualifying intention is not effective in it (until the frankincense is removed from it, below 16:10).
and likewise anything similar to this. For example a sinner's meal-offering with frankincense, or a voluntary meal-offering without oil or frankincense.
an altar that was damaged. And it disqualifies all the slaughtered sacrifices whose blood was not yet sprinkled (above 3:22).
he took the handful of the meal-offering outside. Outside the Temple court.
this intention is nothing. And he takes the handful again when he brings it into the Temple court (above 11:4).
these are things that are not fit etc.. An intention of eating or burning is effective only for things fit for eating or burning (below halakhah 8).
the flesh of sin-offerings that are burned. Which is not burned on the altar and not eaten, but burned outside the city.
and the entire skin of an animal. Even in a burnt-offering, all of whose flesh is burned, its skin is not offered but given to the priests (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 10:14).

except the skin of the fat tail, which is fit for eating. The skin of the fat tail (the tail) is soft and fit for eating, and in every respect it has the law of meat (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 4:21). In sacrifices that are eaten it is eaten, and an intention to eat disqualifies with it; and in a burnt-offering it is burned, and an intention to burn disqualifies with it (Likkutei Halakhot, Zevachim 28a, Even HaAzel).
the bones, sinews, horns and hooves. They are not fit for eating and are not burned, even in a burnt-offering, when they are not attached to meat (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 6:3).
and the hooves. Hoofs.
and the beak. The bill.
and the tips of the wings. The ends of the wings.

even the soft places of all these that are attached to the flesh. These parts, which are not part of the meat but are attached to it, are fit for eating on their side that is attached to the meat and absorbed in it.
for if they were cut from a living animal, the blood would spurt out and flow. When they are separated from the flesh while the animal is alive, blood comes out of them.
are called not fit for eating with regard to sacrifices. But not with regard to the impurity of foods (Hilchot Tumat Okhlin 4:4).
the broth. The gravy of the meat.
and the spices. Onto which meat gathered.
and the shalil. An incompletely formed fetus found in the animal's womb.
and the afterbirth. The membrane in which the fetus is found.
and the eggs of a bird. Found in a bird after slaughter.

none of these is considered with regard to intention in sacrifices. These parts are not considered part of the meat of the sacrifice such that a disqualifying intention concerning them would disqualify the sacrifice (but with regard to eating them, they are like the meat of the sacrifice, and when a disqualifying intention is held about another part of the animal they too become forbidden for eating, below 18:23).

and one may intend with regard to something destined to be destroyed and something destined to be burned. An intention forbids and makes piggul meat that was disqualified and must be destroyed and burned, and it is not considered something unfit for eating (Keren Orah, Me'ilah 7:1).
in one of those four services. In which an intention disqualifies the sacrifice (see above 13:4-6).

he intended that the impure or the disqualified eat... that the impure or the disqualified burn. When he has a disqualifying intention concerning eating something fit for eating or burning something fit for burning, even if he thinks it will be done by those who are not fit, the intention disqualifies.
the sacrifice is piggul, as we have explained. Above 13:1.
and outside the place of eating and burning, it is disqualified and not piggul. Like any intention outside its place.
eating less than an olive's bulk. Eating less than the measure of a k'zayit is not considered eating at all.

and if he expressed it in the language of eating etc.. If he had a disqualifying intention concerning the burning of the sacrificial fats in the language of eating (that he thought the fire would consume them after the time or outside their place), this intention joins an intention concerning the eating of meat.
he intended to eat or burn about half an olive's bulk. Outside its time or outside its place.
in the same intention. An intention of eating or an intention of burning.
whether an intention regarding place or an intention regarding time. His eating and the animal's eating would be outside its time or outside its place.

to eat an olive's bulk over more than the time of eating a half-loaf. He intended to eat outside its time or outside its place and to take, from the start of eating the olive's bulk to its end, longer than the time it takes to eat three eggs' worth. In other laws, when one takes longer than this to eat an olive's bulk, the beginning of the eating does not join the end and he is not considered to have eaten the measure of an olive's bulk (see for example Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 14:8 and elsewhere); but with regard to a disqualifying intention in a sacrifice, the eating joins and the sacrifice is disqualified.

and likewise if he intended an olive's bulk at the time of receiving and an olive's bulk at the time of carrying. The commentators wrote that it seems the text should be emended to: "about half an olive's bulk at the time of receiving and about half an olive's bulk at the time of carrying" (Kesef Mishneh).

for the frankincense with the handful of the meal-offering is like the sacrificial fats of an animal sacrifice. Not only the handful (which is of the kind of the meal-offering) but also the frankincense, which is likewise burned on the altar, is considered like the sacrificial fats of the meal-offering (Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 2:1).
it is piggul, as was explained. Above 13:1-2, 14:5.

once he intended the measure of a sprinkling of the blood, he disqualified. A disqualifying intention concerning sprinkling the blood does not require an olive's bulk; an intention concerning the measure of a single sprinkling of blood suffices to disqualify.
that were slaughtered with the intention of changing the name. He slaughtered a sacrifice not for its own sake (a burnt-offering for the sake of a peace-offering) or not for the sake of its owner.
except that they did not count for the owners as their obligation. And they must bring another sacrifice to fulfill their obligation.
as we have explained. Above 13:3.
when he uprooted the name of the sacrifice intentionally. He knew what the sacrifice was and deliberately changed his intention.
it counted for the owners as their obligation. And although all its services were done for the sake of a peace-offering, he fulfills his obligation of a burnt-offering with it.
for an uprooting by mistake is not an uprooting. And it does not disqualify the sacrifice.
that he pinched it or squeezed out its blood. An intention during these services disqualifies a bird sacrifice (above 13:5).
from a sinner's meal-offering. Which a poor person brings who cannot afford a bird sacrifice that is obligated as a variable sacrifice.
and the meal-offering of jealousy. The meal-offering of the suspected adulteress.
in one of their four services. Taking the handful, placing the handful in a vessel, carrying the handful to the altar, throwing the handful on the fire (above 13:6).
voluntary meal-offerings. One of the meal-offerings that a person may bring as a vow or voluntary offering.
it is forbidden to have an incorrect intention regarding sacrifices, as will be explained. Below 18:1.
for which the verse specified. The Torah indicated concerning them that they must be done for their own sake.
that it be done for the sake of that sin. This change too is considered a change of name and disqualifies the sin-offering (below halakhah 6).
as we have explained. Above halakhah 1.
he slaughtered it for the sake of non-sacred food. For the sake of eating the animal as non-sacred food.

it is valid, but it did not count for the owners. Like the law of changing the name in other sacrifices (other sacrifices slaughtered for the sake of non-sacred food also did not count for the owners, Arukh HaShulchan 150:2).
from oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages in the interpretation of the verses.
that sacrifices profane sacrifices. An intention for the sake of another sacrifice can disqualify the sacrifice.
he slaughtered it for the sake of another sin etc.. See also Hilchot Shegagot 3:3.
a sin-offering that is not fixed. A variable offering.
it is disqualified. For he changed the intention regarding the owner.
he slaughtered it for the sake of another who is obligated a burnt-offering. And he is not obligated a sin-offering.
it is valid, but it did not count for the owners. Like any change of name in other sacrifices.

as it is said, "and he shall atone for him", for him and not for his fellow etc.. From here it is learned that an intention of changing the owner disqualifies only when the sin-offering was done for the sake of another who is obligated a sin-offering.
he slaughtered it for the sake of a dead person. For example, one who was obligated a sin-offering and died before offering it.
for there is no atonement for the dead. And therefore this dead person is not obligated a sin-offering, and slaughtering for his sake does not disqualify.

it is disqualified, lest he be obligated and not know. There is concern lest the person for whose sake the sin-offering was slaughtered is also obligated a sin-offering (and when it is slaughtered for the sake of one who is obligated a burnt-offering, presumably the intent in the slaughter is to bring him out of his obligation of the burnt-offering, which he owes, and therefore the sacrifice is valid, Likkutei Halakhot, Zevachim 7a, Even HaAzel below halakhah 14).
and he intended at the time of slaughter to sprinkle its blood not for its own sake, it is disqualified. Even if in the end he sprinkled it for its own sake.

for one may intend from one service to another. An intention to do something not for its own sake is effective not only in the same act, but even when during one service he intended to perform another service not for its own sake.
that he changed its name for the sake of another sacrifice. That he slaughtered it for the sake of another sacrifice.

as it is said, "And you shall say, It is a Passover sacrifice to the Lord". And when it is slaughtered for the sake of non-sacred food, it is not to the Lord and is therefore disqualified (Kesef Mishneh).

that he slaughtered it at its time, which is the fourteenth of Nisan, even if he slaughtered it in the morning. The time for slaughtering the Passover offering is the afternoon of the 14th of Nisan (Hilchot Korban Pesach 1:4). However, with regard to the intention of changing the name, the entire fourteenth day is considered its time.

he slaughtered it not at its time with the intention of not for its own sake, it is valid. When he slaughtered it not at its time for the sake of another sacrifice, it is not considered a Passover offering, and an intention of changing the name does not disqualify it.

not for the sake of its owners, it is as if it has no owners at its time, and it is disqualified. A Passover offering done not at its time with a change of owners is still considered a Passover offering, and it is disqualified like a Passover offering done at its time not for the sake of its owners.
because it is not its time. The time for its slaughter has not yet arrived. And a Passover offering slaughtered for its own sake not at its time is disqualified (Bavli, Zevachim 8b).

its year passed and he slaughtered it at its time for the sake of a Passover offering etc.. The Passover offering is brought from the flock in its first year; an animal that was sanctified for Passover and entered its second year is disqualified and is offered as a peace-offering (Hilchot Korban Pesach 4:7). If it was slaughtered for the sake of a Passover offering (at its time or not at its time), it has the law of a peace-offering slaughtered not for its own sake, which is valid but did not count for the owners as their obligation.

one who slaughters other sacrifices for the sake of a Passover offering, even if he slaughtered them after midday. An animal sanctified for another sacrifice and slaughtered for the sake of a Passover offering, even at the time of the offering of the Passover sacrifice, is like all sacrifices slaughtered not for their own sake and is valid.
a thanksgiving-offering etc.. The thanksgiving-offering is a peace-offering brought with thanksgiving loaves (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 9:5).
for the thanksgiving-offering is called a peace-offering. ". "And the flesh of the sacrifice of his thanksgiving peace-offerings" (Leviticus 7:15, based on Bavli, Zevachim 4a).
a burnt-offering that he slaughtered for one who is not obligated a sacrifice at all. He slaughtered one person's burnt-offering for the sake of another person who is not obligated a sacrifice.
it did not count for the owners. Like any sacrifice slaughtered with an intention of changing the name.

even though the one for whose sake he slaughtered it is not obligated anything in our eyes. And if he were truly not obligated a sacrifice the intention would not be effective and the owners would fulfill their obligation (Likkutei Halakhot, Zevachim 7a).
for there is no person in Israel who has never transgressed a positive commandment. And is obligated a burnt-offering for atonement (Bavli, Yoma 36a, and see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 3:14).

a burnt-offering that comes after death. For example a person who vowed a burnt-offering and died, and his heirs must bring from his estate the burnt-offering he obligated himself to (see Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:13).
it counted for the owners as their obligation. And the heirs need not bring another sacrifice.
for there are no owners after death. And if so, offering it for the sake of another person is not considered a change.

the two lambs of Atzeret that he slaughtered for the sake of rams. On Shavuot one brings with the two loaves two lambs as peace-offerings (Hilchot Temidin U'Musafin 8:1). If he changed the intent of their slaughter and thought he was slaughtering them for the sake of rams (sheep in their second year; for example he thought to slaughter them for the sake of the two burnt-offering rams that come with the loaves), the lambs are valid but the owners do not fulfill their obligation.
because it is an uprooting by mistake. And it is not an uprooting, as above halakhah 1.

the guilt-offering of a leper. The guilt-offering the leper brings on the day of his purification. Unlike other guilt-offerings, this guilt-offering requires libations (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 2:6).

that he did not put of its blood on the thumbs. Part of the blood of the guilt-offering is received in the priest's hand and sprinkled from it on the lobe of the leper's ear and on the thumbs of his hands and feet (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 4:2). When he did not put of the blood on the thumbs, the sacrifice is valid and the owners have not fulfilled their obligation with it (ibid. 5:2).

requires libations. Although the owners do not fulfill their obligation with it, one brings libations with it as with the guilt-offering of a leper, and does not offer it like other guilt-offerings, which are brought without libations.

for if he offers it without libations, it turns out he is offering a voluntary offering etc.. The guilt-offering was sanctified as the guilt-offering of a leper, and if he offers it without libations it turns out that he is offering it as another guilt-offering as a voluntary offering.
and a guilt-offering does not come as a voluntary offering. Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 14:8.

the lamb that comes with the omer. On the 16th of Nisan the omer meal-offering is offered and a lamb is brought with it as a burnt-offering. Unlike other lambs, which require an issaron of fine flour mixed with a third of a hin of oil, this lamb requires two issarons of fine flour mixed with a third of a hin of oil (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 2:5).

he does not bring its meal-offering of libations of two issarons... for it did not go up for his obligation. Since the owners do not fulfill their obligation with this sacrifice, it is offered as a voluntary burnt-offering and its libations are not doubled.

the tamid offering etc.. With the tamid offering two logs of wood were brought up to add to the fire of the pile (Hilchot Temidin U'Musafin 2:2). When the owners did not fulfill their obligation with the tamid, it is offered as a voluntary burnt-offering and logs of wood are not brought up with it.

or he slaughtered them either before their time or after their time. He slaughtered them before Shavuot or after it. In these cases the lambs are valid, but the owners do not fulfill their obligation by offering them.

and if it was Shabbat, he does not sprinkle. There is a rabbinic prohibition (shevut) against sprinkling the blood, and this prohibition was not permitted on Shabbat in a case where the owners do not fulfill their obligation with the sacrifice (Bavli, Beitzah 20b).

and if he sprinkled, it was accepted, and the fats are burned in the evening. When he sprinkled the blood on Shabbat (in violation), the sacrifice was made acceptable. However, its fats are not burned on Shabbat and one must wait until after Shabbat and then burn them (for a similar law see Hilchot Shegagot 2:14).

they are eaten for a day and a night and do not require bread. Since the owners do not fulfill their obligation with them, bread need not be brought with them, and they are valid like voluntary peace-offerings (see also Hilchot Nezirut 8:12).
the guilt-offering of a nazirite. The guilt-offering brought by a nazirite who became impure.
they are eaten. Like any guilt-offerings.

the peace-offerings of a nazirite. Which the nazirite brings on the day of his purification and brings with bread. Unlike other peace-offerings, which are eaten for two days and one night, the nazirite's peace-offerings are eaten only for a day and a night (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 10:7).
we have already explained etc.. Above 13:1.
when he did not mix with the intention of time another intention. That disqualifies the sacrifice.
the intention of changing the name in the Passover offering and the sin-offering. Above 15:1.

to eat an olive's bulk of something fit for eating outside and an olive's bulk tomorrow. He had an intention of place and an intention of time together in one service; because another disqualifying intention is joined to the intention of time, the sacrifice is not piggul.

about half an olive's bulk outside and about half an olive's bulk tomorrow. An intention of half an olive's bulk does not disqualify (above 14:10). And since there is no full olive's bulk about which he held an intention of time, the sacrifice does not become piggul. However, an intention of half an olive's bulk outside its time and an intention of half an olive's bulk outside its place join, and therefore the sacrifice is disqualified.
and likewise if he mixed the intentions in the burning, it is disqualified and not piggul. For example he intended to burn an olive's bulk outside and an olive's bulk tomorrow.

for half an olive's bulk is not significant next to an olive's bulk. Although an intention of half an olive's bulk outside its place joins half an olive's bulk outside its time to disqualify (as explained in the previous halakhah), it is not counted when there is an intention of a full olive's bulk outside its time.

he intended about half an olive's bulk etc.. In these cases the two halves of an olive's bulk of the intention outside its time join, and the half an olive's bulk of the intention outside its place is not counted.
and similar intentions that do not disqualify, as we have explained. Above 13:8.
and he mixed with them the intention of time. In addition to the intention of placing the blood not in its place, he intended to eat or burn tomorrow.
it is piggul. Since no other disqualifying intention is mixed with the intention of time.
and since we have explained in these halakhot that the blood that was placed etc.. Above 2:10.
does not permit the meat for eating, as we have explained. For when the blood is placed not in its place, the owners fulfill their obligation but the meat of the sacrifice is disqualified (there).

and any sprinkling that does not permit the meat for eating, if he intended to give it outside its time, he did not make it piggul. Only in a case where all the services of the sacrifice were done properly does the sacrifice become piggul through an intention outside its time; but when the sprinkling is not valid and does not permit the meat for eating (even if it atoned), the sacrifice does not become piggul (see below 18:16).

therefore if he again intended an intention of time in this sacrifice, it is disqualified and not piggul. Since the intention of giving the blood not in its proper place outside its time disqualified the sacrifice, another intention outside its time held in this sacrifice (even in a manner fit to make a valid sacrifice piggul, such as an intention to give the blood in its place or burn the fats tomorrow) does not make it piggul (like any intention outside its time mixed with another intention, above halakhah 1).
gathering the frankincense. Collecting the frankincense on the meal-offering in order to put it in a vessel and burn it together with the handful.

and it is not piggul until he holds the intention of time in the entire permitter. An intention outside its time makes piggul only if he held it both when he performed the service with the handful and when he performed the service with the frankincense, since both together permit the meal-offering for eating (see above 13:3).
their sprinkling. Their burning on the altar.

for burning does not make burning piggul. An intention of piggul at the time of burning one part of the permitter, to burn its other part outside its time, is not enough to make piggul, since at the time of burning the other part no intention of piggul was held (see Hazon Ish).
for one does not make piggul with half a permitter. Above halakhah 7.

but if he burned the handful alone and intended etc.. Although an intention at the time of burning the handful to burn the frankincense tomorrow does not make piggul by itself (as explained at the beginning of the halakhah), and an intention at the time of burning the frankincense also does not make piggul by itself, the combination of the two intentions makes piggul.

he burned a shumshum's worth of the handful with the frankincense... until he completed the entire handful with the frankincense. He burned the handful and frankincense little by little and held an intention outside its time during the burning.
rather it is like a meal-offering whose handful was not burned. And therefore the meal-offering is disqualified.

a sinner's meal-offering or a meal-offering of jealousy that had frankincense on it. And at that time they are not fit for offering, and an intention of piggul does not make them piggul (see also above 14:3).
remainders that became deficient between the taking of the handful and the burning. And their law is that he burns the handful but the remainders are forbidden to eat (above 11:20).
it is a doubt whether they were fixed as piggul. Since the burning did not permit the remainders for eating, there is a doubt whether it is effective to make them piggul or not.

all the bloods that are placed on the outer altar etc.. Even sacrifices from whose blood one must sprinkle on the altar more than once are valid if he gave of their blood only once (above 2:1), and therefore after the first placing, a disqualifying intention does not disqualify in the remaining placings.

since the first presentation is the main one. Therefore thoughts during the other presentations are not counted as thoughts mixed with the thought of piggul that disqualify but do not render piggul (above 16:1).
the blood that is placed on the inner altar. The sin offerings that are burned.
since all of them are indispensable to one another, as we have explained. For if one omitted a single application, the offering is disqualified (above 2:3).
he spoiled it with the thought. He had a disqualifying thought regarding it.
if he had the thought at the first one etc.. In the inner sin offerings.

it is disqualified but it is not piggul, until he sprinkles all of them with the thought of the time. The offering is piggul only if he had the thought of beyond its time during the whole of the permitting rite (above 16:7); therefore it is not piggul until he has the thought of the time during all the sprinklings.
for all of them are one application. All the sprinklings of the inner sin offerings are considered one application, since all of them are indispensable.

and dipping the finger in the blood in the inner sin offerings renders it piggul. In sprinkling the blood of the sin offerings one must dip the finger in the blood in the vessel before each sprinkling (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:8). A thought at the time of dipping the finger in the inner sin offerings disqualifies the offering and renders it piggul, just as the sprinkling does (but not in the outer sin offerings; Babylonian Talmud, Zevachim 14a).
in something done inside. The sprinklings of blood done in the Sanctuary building.
in something done outside. The slaughtering of the sin offerings, the pouring out of the remainder of the blood, and the burning of the sacrificial parts, which are done in the Temple court.

if he was standing in the Sanctuary and said etc.. Just as a thought in the court does not take effect regarding a rite done inside, so a thought in the Sanctuary does not take effect regarding a rite done in the court.

the thanksgiving offering renders the bread piggul etc.. The loaves that come with the thanksgiving offering are secondary to the offering; therefore when he has a thought of piggul regarding the offering, the loaves also become piggul, but when he has a thought of piggul regarding the bread, the meat does not become piggul.
and the same law applies to the two lambs of Shavuot with the two loaves that come with them. For the two loaves that come with the peace offerings on Shavuot are secondary to them.
to eat a k'zayit of the meat of the sacrifice with the bread on the next day. To eat a k'zayit, part of it from the meat and part from the bread.
the bread alone is piggul. For the thought about the meat combines with the thought about the bread, and there is here a thought of piggul regarding a k'zayit.

the two bowls of frankincense that accompany the showbread etc.. Burning the bowls of frankincense permits the eating of the loaves; therefore a thought of beyond its time while burning them renders the loaves piggul.
both of them are piggul. The two loaves are considered one body; therefore if one became piggul the other is also piggul (Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 2:2).
both rows are piggul. The showbread was arranged on the table in two stacks, and both are considered one body.
that loaf and that row are forbidden, and the pure one eats it in its purity. See also above 12:14.
until he has the thought during the whole of the permitting rite. As above 16:7.

these combine to make piggul. Since the two lambs together permit the two loaves together, the thought he had at the first lamb about the first loaf combines with the thought he had at the second lamb about the second loaf.

with the two bowls and the two rows. That is, while burning one bowl he thought of eating from one of the rows on the next day, and while burning the second bowl he thought of eating from the second row on the next day.
if he had the thought of the time regarding one of the two lambs. In offering or eating the lamb (and not the loaves).

the one he did with the thought of the time is piggul and the second is valid. Although the two lambs together permit the two loaves, each of them is considered a separate offering, and if one is disqualified the other remains valid (and the bread is disqualified but does not become piggul, since he rendered piggul only one lamb, which is only part of its permitting rite).
for one does not have a thought of one regarding the other. For they are two separate offerings.

the two lambs of Shavuot sanctify the bread only through slaughter. The slaughter sanctifies the loaves with the sanctity of the body of the offering (so that they become disqualified by being left overnight and the like).

if he slaughtered them and threw their blood with the thought of changing the name, the bread is not sanctified. Since the lambs were not slaughtered for their own sake, the slaughter does not sanctify the bread (for a similar law regarding the loaves of a thanksgiving offering see above 12:18).

if he slaughtered them for their own sake and threw their blood not for their own sake, the bread is sanctified and not sanctified. The bread was sanctified by the slaughter, but since the blood was not thrown for their sake, the bread is not permitted for eating (Kesef Mishneh).
that went out. From the Temple court.
and he threw the blood of the lambs with the thought of the time. While they were outside.

the two loaves became piggul even though they are outside. Although the two loaves were disqualified by having gone outside the court, the thought of beyond its time renders them piggul, and one is liable to karet for eating them.

for the throwing of the blood takes effect for one that went out even though it is still outside. Although the blood was thrown while the bread was outside and disqualified from eating, the throwing of the blood was done properly, and therefore one is liable to karet for eating them (see below 18:16).

the lambs of Shavuot that he slaughtered for their own sake, and the bread was lost etc.. After the lambs were waved with the bread they were fixed together, and if one of them is lost the other is disqualified (Hilchot Temidin U'Musafin 8:15). Therefore when the blood is thrown for their sake the lambs are disqualified, since their bread was lost. However, if he threw the blood not for the sake of communal peace offerings but for the sake of individual peace offerings, there is room for doubt whether the lambs might be permitted for eating, since individual peace offerings do not require bread.

he threw their blood with the thought of the time. The wording is difficult, and some emended it: "he threw their blood not for their own sake" (Kesef Mishneh in the name of the Rikvu, who also brings another explanation). Others explained that the "thought of the time" mentioned here means for the sake of individual peace offerings, which are eaten for two days and a night, in contrast to the lambs of Shavuot, which are communal peace offerings and are eaten for a day and a night (Mirkevet HaMishneh).
a thought that is not proper regarding sacrifices. A disqualifying thought.
from oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages in the interpretation of the verses.
for this is similar to inflicting a blemish on sacrificial animals. And one who inflicts a blemish on sacrificial animals receives lashes (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 1:7).
for thought is not an act. And one does not receive lashes for a transgression unless it involves an actual act (Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:1-2).

from oral tradition they learned that the verse warns only about disqualified consecrated items. For an offering with a blemish is called an "abomination" (Deuteronomy 17:1), and this includes all disqualified consecrated items (Sifrei, Re'eh, section 99).

and similarly, for consecrated animals in which a blemish was inflicted, one who eats a k'zayit of them receives lashes. For it is forbidden to eat a consecrated animal with a blemish before it is redeemed, and when he inflicted a blemish on it they penalized him by not allowing it to be redeemed (Avraham Yigal).
until another blemish develops in them and they are eaten with their blemish. After their redemption.
as we have explained. Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 1:10.
that became piggul through the thought of the time, as we have explained. Above 13:1.
a fixed sin offering. One that always comes from an animal, in contrast to the "ascending and descending" offering, which varies according to the person's financial situation (Hilchot Shegagot 1:4).

one is liable to karet only for eating things that were permitted, whether to a person or to the altar. In the process of offering, some parts of the offering are burned on the altar and other parts are eaten. Only the parts that were permitted to the altar or to a person by a rite performed on other parts of the offering ("the permitting rite," see above 13:3) are considered piggul and one is liable to karet for eating them. But for eating the permitting rite itself, or offerings that are offered whole and have no permitting rites, one is not liable to karet.
he receives lashes like one who eats disqualified consecrated items in which there is no piggul. As explained above in halachah 3.

the flesh of the sin offerings that are burned. Since the flesh is burned outside the city and is neither burned on the altar nor eaten by a person, it is not among the things permitted for human eating or for the altar, and there is no piggul in it (see also above 13:8).
and the meal offerings that are burned. The meal offering of a kohen and the meal offering of libations, which are burned entirely.

and the wine, whether wine that comes etc.. The wine poured on the altar, whether it is part of the libations of the offerings (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 2:1) or brought by itself as a vow or a freewill offering (ibid. 14:1).

and the log of oil of the leper. The leper brings a log of oil with his guilt offering, and after some of it is sprinkled toward the Holy of Holies and some is placed on the ear lobe and thumbs of the leper, the rest of the oil is eaten by the kohanim (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 4:2).
is not dependent on it etc.. The leper is not obligated to bring the log of oil with the guilt offering but may bring it later; if so, the guilt offering does not permit the oil.
as will be explained in its place. Ibid. 5:4.
and one who leaves over does not receive lashes. See also Hilchot Korban Pesach 10:11.

the verse converted it to a positive commandment. The prohibition ("you shall not leave over") was transferred to become a positive commandment ("you shall burn it with fire"), and one does not receive lashes for it.

if they are most holy offerings. Those that are eaten on the day of offering and the night after it (and the same applies to the thanksgiving offering and the ram of a nazirite, which are also eaten for a day and a night).

once the dawn rises. The beginning of the lightening of the eastern sky before sunrise (about an hour and a fifth before it - Commentary on the Mishnah, Berakhot 1:1). By the words of the Sages the meat is already forbidden from midnight (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 10:8).
and if they are lesser holy offerings. Those that are eaten until the end of the day after the offering.
from the sunset of the second day. From the offering of the sacrifice.

and where does the verse warn about piggul and about leftover. In the verses cited above the punishment of karet for eating piggul and leftover was stated, but the commandment prohibiting eating them was not explained.

for it is said there: he shall not eat, for they are holy. The verse quoted speaks of the prohibition against a non-kohen eating consecrated items, and it seems that the intent is the following verse (Exodus 29:34) which speaks of the prohibition against eating the remaining inauguration offerings: "and you shall burn the remainder with fire; it shall not be eaten, for it is holy" (see the section on textual variants in the Frankel edition).

and piggul and leftover combine with each other to make a k'zayit. If he ate half a k'zayit of piggul and half a k'zayit of leftover, he is liable to karet, for both are included in the same warning (see Babylonian Talmud, Me'ilah 17b).

and all the piggul and leftover items combine. If one knowingly ate a k'zayit of piggul or leftover from several kinds of offerings, he is liable to karet, and if he did so unintentionally, he is liable to a sin offering.
to cause them to become impure. To cause them impurity.
for he disqualifies them. As above, halachah 2.
and the same applies to the other offerings etc.. The verse deals with the meat of a peace offering, and from it we learn about the other offerings, and not only about meat.
before atonement or after atonement. The throwing of the blood.

with a primary source of impurity. For example, one impure from a corpse, a carcass or a creeping creature (for the list of primary sources of impurity see Maimonides' introduction to the Order of Taharot).
with a derivative of impurity. Something that became impure by touching a primary source of impurity.

with impurities of rabbinic origin. For example, one who became impure from gentiles (see Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav U'Moshav 2:10; for the list of impurities of rabbinic origin see Maimonides' introduction to the Order of Taharot).
lashes for rebellion. Lashes by rabbinic decree.
the impurity for which one is liable to karet for entering the Temple. See Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 3:13.
an ascending and descending offering. A sin offering whose type varies according to the person's financial situation (Hilchot Shegagot 1:4).

and how do we know that it speaks only of impurity of the body. How do we know that the words "and his impurity is upon him" refer to the impure person who ate, and not to the impure meat that was eaten.

as it is said: and a person who touches any impure thing. And in this verse it is explicit that it speaks of an impure person who ate and thereby incurs karet, and from this it follows that the verse before it also speaks of the impure person.
and the same applies to the other offerings of the altar. The verse was stated regarding peace offerings, and the same law applies to the other offerings.
and where does it warn about this sin. See above, halachah 10.

from oral tradition they learned that this is a warning to the impure person not to eat consecrated food. The Sages learned through tradition that it speaks of eating consecrated food and not only of touching it.

after he immersed but before nightfall. Even after immersion, a mild impurity remains on the impure person until the end of the day (and during this time he is called a "tevul yom," Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 10:1-2).

before he brings his atonement offering. Those lacking atonement (a zav, a zavah, a woman after childbirth or a leper) who became pure of their impurity and have not yet brought the offering that completes their purification process (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:1).
that all his impurity be upon him. And a tevul yom and one lacking atonement have begun their purification process.

and similarly, if he ate from the flesh of the sin offerings that are burned while impure, after their blood was thrown. For only after the blood is thrown can the meat be burned in the proper manner outside the camp.

it has already been explained to you etc.. From the totality of what was said in this chapter - that one is not liable for piggul on something that has no permitting rite (above halachah 7), and that one is liable for impurity even on something that has no permitting rite from the time it was sanctified in a vessel (above halachah 16) - it is clear that there are things for which one is not liable for piggul but is liable for leftover and impurity.

except for blood, for which one is never liable except for blood alone. For eating blood one is liable to karet on account of eating blood (which is forbidden even in an unconsecrated animal, Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 1:6), and not because of the prohibition of leftover or impure.
an impure person who ate sacrificial parts is liable to karet. Even though the sacrificial parts are burned and not eaten.
a Pesach offering that was not roasted. The Pesach offering is eaten roasted and may not be eaten before roasting (Hilchot Korban Pesach 8:4).

and the loaves of a thanksgiving offering from which the challah was not separated. The loaves of the thanksgiving offering are eaten by the owners after one separates from each kind one loaf for the kohen (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 9:21).

even though they are not yet fit for what they are meant for. Although they cannot yet actually be eaten, they are considered consecrated items whose permitting rites were offered, and one is liable for eating them while impure.
leftover is what remains of an offering that was offered properly, after its time of eating. But an offering that was disqualified does not become leftover.
who mixed them together and ate them. He mixed them and ate the mixture.

even though one kind is greater than the other etc.. In a mixture of forbidden and permitted food, when most of the mixture is permitted (and the forbidden does not impart taste), the forbidden is nullified by the majority and the whole mixture is permitted (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 15:6). However, when several prohibitions are mixed, the smaller prohibition is not nullified by the majority, and one who eats from it transgresses all the prohibitions.

and piggul or leftover or impure that he brought up to the top of the altar. Although one should not initially bring up meat and sacrificial parts that were disqualified, if they were brought up they are to be burned (above 3:7).
their prohibition is removed from them. There is no prohibition of karet for eating them, and one who eats them does not receive lashes.

and the sacrificial parts combine with the meat. Although the sacrificial parts are burned on the altar and the meat is eaten, they combine together to reach the amount of eating that makes one liable.

and he ate from it, from the hide etc.. Things that are not fit for eating, or whose eating is not significant and is not considered eating regarding offerings (above 14:7, where the details mentioned here were explained).
the fetus. An incompletely formed offspring found in its mother's womb.
the afterbirth. The membrane in which the fetus is found.

he is liable for piggul, leftover and impure as one who eats from the rest of the meat of the sacrifice.
