Although a thought of piggul regarding a fetus or afterbirth does not disqualify or render the offering piggul (above 14:7), eating them is significant, and when a thought of piggul was had regarding another part of the animal they too became piggul, and one is liable for them.
consecrated items of gentiles. Offerings that were consecrated by gentiles.
and similarly, the blood of consecrated items, as we have explained. Above, halachah 17.

and similarly frankincense, incense and wood, one is not liable to karet for them. Since they are not fit for eating (but if they are impure and he ate them, he is liable to lashes, above halachah 12).
and the flesh that touches any impure thing. And the verse continues: "shall be burned with fire."

an offering that became piggul or was disqualified is burned in the Temple immediately. When the body of the offering itself was disqualified; but when the disqualification is in the owners (for example, they became impure) or in the blood (for example, it was spilled), it is left until its form changes (Melekhet Shlomo, and see Hilchot Korban Pesach 4:3).
its form changes. They wait until it spoils and then burn it.

bulls and goats that are burned. The sin offerings that are burned (for their definition see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 1:16). When they are done as commanded their flesh is burned outside the city, and if they were disqualified in the court, their flesh is burned in the court like all disqualified items (ibid. 7:3).
and going out before the time arrives for them to go out. Before the blood is thrown.

and similarly, if half the animal went out with most of a limb etc.. When half of the animal went out, and in the part that went out there is a limb most of which is outside and a minority of which is still inside, there is a doubt whether the minority of the limb is joined to its majority, so that most of the animal is outside and it is disqualified, or whether it is not joined and only half the animal is outside.

and three went out and two remained, and the three took out half the animal. There is a doubt whether we look only at the animal, most of which did not go out, or also at those carrying the animal, and since most of them went out with half of the animal, it is disqualified.
meat found in the court. And it is not known what it is.

limbs are burnt offerings and pieces are sin offerings. The meat of a burnt offering is burned entirely on the altar, and therefore it is cut into whole limbs and not into small pieces (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 6:19). The meat of a sin offering is eaten, and therefore it is cut into small pieces.

and what is found in Jerusalem is peace offerings. Since most of the animals in Jerusalem were offerings, we assume the meat is consecrated. And since the meat of most holy offerings may not be taken out of the court, we assume that the meat is of peace offerings, which are eaten throughout Jerusalem.

for whoever transgressed and ate. A non-kohen who ate the meat found in Jerusalem and a kohen who ate what was found in pieces in the court are exempt, and a non-kohen who ate what was found in the court or a kohen who ate what was found as limbs in the court are liable (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shekalim 7:3; the commentators disagreed whether this is liability for lashes or liability regarding me'ilah).

even though peace offerings are forbidden for eating from the beginning of the third night. Peace offerings are eaten on the day of slaughter and the day after, and already at the beginning of the third night they are forbidden for eating and become leftover.
whether in its time or not in its time. Even when they are not burned on the third day but afterward, they must be burned specifically during the day.
and burning impure, leftover and piggul does not override a festival. Rather, we wait until the next day and then burn them.
one burns it inside. In the court, in the place designated for burning consecrated items (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:3).
one burns it outside. And we do not bring it inside to burn it like other disqualified items, so as not to bring impurity into the court.
with a primary source of impurity... with a derivative of impurity. See above 18:12.

for it is first-degree impure. The derivative impurities are divided by their degree of impurity: one who touches a primary source of impurity is called first, one who touches the first is called second, one who touches the second is called third, and one who touches the third is called fourth (Hilchot Tum'at Met 5:8).
meat that became impure through a derivative of a derivative of impurity, since it is third. Meat that became impure by touching a second and became third.

for a third that touched a first becomes a second, as will be explained in its place. A third-degree impure item that touched a first-degree one becomes second-degree impure (Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 4:15).

oil that was disqualified through a tevul yom, which is third. Oil that touched a tevul yom (an impure person who immersed and the evening has not yet come) became impure through him and became third-degree impure (Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 10:3).

with a metal lamp that was touched by one impure from a corpse, for the lamp is a primary source etc.. One impure from a corpse who touches a metal vessel makes it a primary source of impurity like himself (Hilchot Tum'at Met 3:2), and the oil touching it becomes first-degree impure.
one is not careful about adding to it. Once there is impurity, one is not careful not to add further impurity to it.

the leftover of lesser holy offerings, its owners burn it in their homes. Lesser holy offerings are eaten throughout the city. When they became leftover, the place of their disqualification is in the city, and therefore they are burned there.
and he remembered that he has consecrated meat in his hand. Of lesser holy offerings that was disqualified by leaving the city, and he must burn it.

if he passed Mount Scopus, he burns it where he is. When he has gone far from Jerusalem, beyond Mount Scopus (or the same distance in another direction), they did not trouble him to return, and he may burn it where he is.
and if not, if there is in it etc.. When he is closer and there is a k'zayit or more of meat in his hand, he must return to the city and burn the meat in the city, at the place where it was eaten.

and if he is a guest who has no house, he burns it in front of the Birah. At the place of burning on the Temple Mount (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:4. In this place they also burned the meat of the Pesach offering that became impure, Hilchot Korban Pesach 4:3).
from the wood of the altar's arrangement. If they burn with their own wood and take the remaining wood, they will be suspected of stealing from the wood of the altar's arrangement (ibid.).
and all bones of consecrated items that have no marrow do not require burning. A bone is not considered meat, and therefore even when the offering was disqualified, it does not require burning.

except for the bones of the Pesach offering. Which are burned even when they have no marrow, since it is forbidden to break the bones of the Pesach offering, and therefore all the bones of the Pesach offering are burned so that no mishap occurs and they not be broken (see Hilchot Korban Pesach 10:2 and the commentary there).
we have already explained. Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:20.
the hide belongs to the kohanim. In most holy offerings.
a sacrifice that was flayed and found to be a treifah. Since it became clear that it was disqualified even before the flaying, they did not acquire its hide, and it must be burned.

that was disqualified through the thought of the time or the thought of the place. And this speaks of a case where he had the disqualifying thought before the flaying (Rikvu; and in the opinion of Likkutei Halachot, Zevachim 104a, in the case of a disqualifying thought the hide is burned even when the disqualification came after the hide was flayed).
as we have explained. That whenever the altar acquired its meat (it was valid at the time the blood was thrown), they acquired its hide (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:19).
and a sacrifice that was flayed before the throwing is not disqualified. And after the blood is thrown they acquire it (Rikvu, Kesef Mishneh).
consecrated meat that became impure or leftover or disqualified, and likewise the meal offering. Above, halachah 1.

and a conditional guilt offering that he learned he had not sinned before its blood was thrown. That when he learned that he had not sinned before the blood was thrown, it must be burned, as above 4:19. [Note: the text here is as it appears in the printed editions, and in the manuscript the text is: "that he learned he had not sinned after its blood was thrown," which is apparently a scribal error. See the Rikvu, who suggested emending in other ways.]
and the bird sin offering that comes for a doubt. Above 7:10.

and the hair of a pure nazirite. Who shaves his hair on the day he completes his nazirite period after bringing the offerings, and burns it in the fire when he cooks the peace offering he brings (Hilchot Nezirut 8:2-3).
and orlah. The fruit of a fruit tree in the first three years after its planting is forbidden for benefit (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 10:9).
and kilayim of the vineyard. Vegetables or grain sown beside vines, or a vine planted beside vegetables; both are forbidden for benefit (Hilchot Kilayim 5:7).
and something that is not normally burned etc.. See also Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 16:27.
consecrated animals that died. See also Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 5:12.
consecrated items of the altar. Consecrated animals designated for offering.
consecrated items for the upkeep of the Temple. Animals consecrated for the needs of the Temple, not for offering.
and consecrated animals that miscarried, the miscarried fetus is buried; if they miscarried an afterbirth, it is buried. See also Hilchot Temurah 4:10.
and the ox that is stoned. Whose law is to be stoned (for example, one that killed a person) and is forbidden for benefit (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 4:22).

and the heifer whose neck is broken. When a slain person is found on the road and it is not known who killed him, they measure the distance from him to the surrounding cities, and the elders of the closest city bring a heifer and break its neck as atonement (Hilchot Rotze'ach 9:2-3). The heifer is forbidden for benefit and is buried (ibid. 10:6).

and the birds of the leper. A leper who is becoming pure of his impurity brings two wild birds; one of the birds is slaughtered over a vessel containing living water, and this bird is forbidden for benefit and buried (Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at 11:1).

and the hair of an impure nazirite. A nazirite who became impure must bring offerings, shave his hair and begin his nazirite period anew; his hair is forbidden for benefit and requires burial (Hilchot Nezirut 6:14).

and the firstborn of a donkey. The firstborn offspring of a donkey must be redeemed with a lamb and given to a kohen. When the owner does not wish to redeem the donkey, its neck is broken, and it is forbidden for benefit and requires burial (Hilchot Bikkurim 12:4).
and meat in milk. See also Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 9:1.
and unconsecrated animals slaughtered in the Temple court. See also Hilchot Shechitah 2:2.
a full sit. The distance between the thumb and the forefinger, about two handbreadths (Hilchot Shabbat 9:7).

of the hair of a nazirite and of the firstborn of a donkey, in sackcloth, it is burned. Only when the hair of the impure nazirite and the hair of the firstborn donkey are by themselves is their law burial, but when they are woven into a garment their law is burning, so that no one will dig after it and take it out (Rikvu in the name of the Yerushalmi).
those that are buried, their ashes are forbidden. It is forbidden to benefit from them even after they have decayed and rotted.

except for the ashes of the outer altar and the inner altar and the cleanings of the menorah. The ashes of the outer altar and the inner altar and the ashes of the menorah (see also Hilchot Me'ilah 2:14-15).

even though he is stringent regarding their burning, he is lenient regarding their ashes. Although when he burns those that are to be buried he is stringent on himself by not being satisfied with burial, he should not do so, because for those that are burned there is a lenient aspect, that their ashes are permitted.
he was offering with him among the sacrifices etc.. See also Hilchot Tefillin 1:18, Hilchot Ma'aser 12:18, Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav U'Moshav 13:8.
Israel is not suspected of this. Of lying and forbidding what is permitted.
but if he said to him. Some time later.

the sacrifices that I offered for you on that day. And this speaks of a case where he could have told him once and did not tell him (and therefore his credibility is in doubt). But if he did not see him, and the first time he saw him he told him, he is believed just as he is believed at the time of the act (Rikvu and Kesef Mishneh, based on Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav U'Moshav there, and see Mar'eh HaKorbanot and Mirkevet HaMishneh, Hilchot Ma'aser 12:18).
